rationale: A wins because it is better at showing the founder what proof has to exist before anyone should pitch, especially in “Paying Users Are Down. Bumble Is Betting AI Changes That.” B is cleaner, but it gets too cute with “Bumble is asking investors to buy a turnaround story written by an algorithm” and too loose with “AI matchmaking just went mainstream.” A still needs a pruning knife; its fourth angle wanders into category claims it has not earned.
gaps_in_A: “Bumble is the highest-profile dating platform to deploy AI matchmaking and AI-assisted message writing at scale” is not in the update. That is the kind of confident overreach that gets a pitch killed in the first reply.

“If AI Writes the First Message, Is Bumble's Women-First Model Still Feminist?” is sharp, but “feminist” imports brand ideology not supplied in the facts. The safer, stronger version is the agency/authenticity tension.

“Users Push Back as Dating Apps Embrace AI Matchmaking” turns one Bumble relaunch plus unspecified criticism into a plural category trend. It admits it needs outside proof, but the headline has already spent the money.
The founder angle says “the AI relaunch is the first major move under her return.” Plausible, but not supplied. Flag it as a question unless you have the timeline.
gaps_in_B: “AI matchmaking just went mainstream” is an unsupported conclusion. One major public company adopting AI is evidence, not a coronation.
“category-standard feature” is worse: that requires competitor evidence the update explicitly does not provide. B knows this because its own proof section asks for it.
“funding-mechanics” is the wrong story type. Bumble is public; this is markets/turnaround, not funding mechanics. Sloppy label, small wound, but avoidable.

“brand promise is that its message-first model empowers authentic connection” fuses two supplied facts into one polished claim. Women-message-first is supplied; authenticity is user criticism, not necessarily Bumble’s promise.
